title: I built a game studio to automate all the jobs
author: tanepiper
selftext:
How do you run a game studio when you're the only person in it? You build a fully #agentic system to manage your fleet of #AI

I started Teskooano, a 3D space simulator, in April 2025. Accurate physics, using both real data and procedural planets, and much more .

For the first year and a half it was me and Cursor in bursts - a busy summer, then long quiet stretches when life and work got in the way. About 660 commits in eighteen months.

At the end of October I moved it to Claude  Code. There have been around 2,600 commits since then, most of them this month.

Same project but what changed is that I stopped pairing with one assistant and started running it as a team that coordinates across the day to get shit done.

Most days there are a dozen sessions going at once, each starting its own agents - one on an orbit bug, one writing shaders, one filming a trailer, one reviewing what the other three did. It works like a real studio - but it was getting messy without a way for every agent to report back to a central control.

So together with the AI I built the studio dashboard as a way to see what my team is up to, and communicate without interrupting.

\- What it costs. Every session, agent and module has a running cost, including the money spent on branches that never got merged. A real studio has a finance department; mine has a page I try not to look at too often.

\- Who's who. There are 48 specialist agents now - art, code and infrastructure directors, programmers for physics, GPU and terrain, reviewers, and even a finance analyst and a legal researcher (who only gives advice but looks into things like IP rights or GDPR). 

\- A family tree shows which session started which agent, so when something breaks I can trace it back to whoever did it.

\- Not overloading the system. One laptop, lots of agents who all want a dev server, the test suite and a Blender render at the same time. The machine lock gives each heavy job a slot, and the rest wait their turn.

\- Everyone uses the same tools. The dashboard is also an MCP server with 41 tools, next to the ones for the asset editor, the game, Cloudflare and Sentry. The agents see what I see, leave me notes, answer my feedback and suggest improvements to how they work.

I'm still the boss. Agents can suggest; only I approve. They can't push, deploy or commit outside their own branch, and everything goes in an audit log.

\- Saying it once. If I tell one session "film with the UI off", it becomes a studio rule, and every agent gets it when it starts. Like a handbook, except they actually read it.

The dashboard is mostly written by the team it now manages, which still feels a bit odd.

Opus and Fable didn't change what I was building. It changed how fast it moves, and at that speed the hard part stops being the code and becomes keeping track of everything. If you're one person trying to make something far too big, it turns out the answer is the same as everyone else's: build a studio.
